definition: The study of substances: what they are made of, what properties they have and how they can be changed into other substances.
Everything that has mass and takes up space, for example solids, liquids and gases. Everything you can touch is made of matter.
A particular kind of matter, for example water, iron, sugar or oxygen. A substance has definite properties.
A thing that is made of some substance. A spoon is an object, and the steel it is made of is the substance.
Another word for a substance, especially one that is made or used in products. Water and salt are chemicals.
The level where you see, feel and measure, for example that the water in a beaker has a certain temperature and mass.
The level where you explain with atoms, molecules and ions, which you cannot see but can only imagine using a model.
The level where you write with chemical symbols, formulas and mathematics, for example H₂O and ρ = m / V.
A way of finding things out: ask a question that can be answered, guess with a hypothesis, test with a fair investigation and draw a conclusion.
The question that an investigation is meant to answer. It must be possible to answer it with measurements or observations.
An explanatory guess that can be tested, often written as “If … then … because …”.
The sum of all the measured values divided by the number of measured values. It is used to get a more reliable result when you have repeated an experiment.
Something that may have made the results less reliable, for example an uneven measurement or something not being kept the same.
How much you can trust the result. It gets higher if you repeat the experiment and keep everything the same except one thing.
Something that can be changed or measured in an investigation.
What you change on purpose in an investigation. Only one thing should be changed at a time.
What you measure in an investigation, and which you think is affected by what you change.
A variable that is kept the same in all the experiments, so that the comparison is fair.
What you actually see, measure or hear. It is different from the interpretation of what it means.
An explanation that has been tested in many ways by many scientists and has stood up to scrutiny.
A simplified picture that helps us understand and predict, for example the particle model, where substances are drawn as small balls.
Thinking things through before you start: what can go wrong, how serious and how likely is it, and what can I do to reduce the risk.
A symbol on a diamond shape with a red border that shows what kind of hazard a chemical product has. There are nine in the EU system.
The word Danger or Warning on a label. Danger is used for the most serious hazards and Warning for less serious ones.
A hazard statement on a label that describes how the product is dangerous, for example H302: Harmful if swallowed.
A precautionary statement on a label with advice on safe handling, for example P102: Keep out of reach of children.
A gas burner used in the chemistry lab. With the air ring closed the flame is yellow, and with it open the flame is blue and hotter.
A text that tells what you investigated, how you did it, what results you got and what conclusion you draw, so that someone else can repeat the experiment.
Something you can see, measure or test in a substance, for example colour, density and melting point.
A property that you can observe or measure without the substance changing into something else, for example colour, density and melting point.
A property that describes how a substance reacts with other substances and forms new ones, for example that it burns or rusts.
How much mass a substance has per volume, ρ = m / V, often in g/cm³. An object floats in a liquid if its density is lower than that of the liquid.
An old mixture of experiments and philosophy that, among other things, tried to make gold from base metals. Chemistry grew out of it.
A prize that is awarded every year, since 1901, according to Alfred Nobel's will, in chemistry among other fields.
